title: Conquer yourself (103–108)
hook: one who conquers himself is greater than one who conquers a thousand times a thousand in battle

segments.voice: Yesterday, sahassa, one word of peace, and your line: one word that calms. Did you say your useful sentence? Day one hundred seventy-nine.

The Buddha grew up among warriors. He was born into a ruling family, trained, the stories say, in the arts of a prince, and he lived in a world of kings who measured greatness by battles won and lands taken. In that world, a conqueror meant one thing. So when he wanted to describe the greatest victory a person could win, he borrowed their language, and then turned it completely around. Today, verses one hundred three to one hundred eight: conquer yourself.
screen: `BORN AMONG WARRIORS.` → `GREATNESS MEASURED IN BATTLES.` → `THE LANGUAGE, TURNED AROUND.`

segments.voice: Verse one hundred three, in Müller's English: “If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.” A thousand times a thousand: a million enemies. And one person, sitting quietly, who has won against their own anger, their own craving, their own fog. The verse says that second person is the greater conqueror. Why? Verses one hundred four and one hundred five explain. Victory over yourself is better than victory over everyone else, and no one can take it back. Not a god, not a heavenly musician, not Mara, not even Brahma, can turn that victory into defeat. A king's victories can be undone in a single battle. Land is lost; alliances break; the next king comes. But a mind that has truly let go of hatred doesn't have to win that fight again. Verses one hundred six to one hundred eight add a surprising comparison: a hundred years of ritual sacrifice is worth less than honoring, for a single moment, one person whose mind is well trained. The conquest the verse describes needn't be dramatic. It's small, daily, and mostly invisible. Not snapping at your kid. Putting the phone down. Letting a grudge go for the fourth time this week. Nobody writes songs about those battles. But the Dhammapada calls conquering yourself the greatest victory. And one of the Buddha's titles carries the same idea: the Jina, the conqueror. Not of lands. Of himself.
screen: `A MILLION ENEMIES, OR ONE SELF.` · `A VICTORY NO ONE CAN UNDO.` · `A MOMENT OVER A HUNDRED YEARS.` · `SMALL, DAILY, INVISIBLE.` · then, large: `THE GREATEST CONQUEST.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of one small inner fight you keep losing. Reaching for the phone. The sharp reply. The second helping you don't want. The spiral of worry at night. Just one. Now, while you breathe, picture the moment it usually starts: the first itch, the first flare. See yourself noticing it, and pausing for one breath before acting. That pause is the whole battle. Nothing heroic, just one breath. Rest here, and let the body feel what it's like to win that small, quiet fight. The bell holds the time.
Conquer yourself. One who wins over their own mind is greater than one who conquers a million in battle, and that victory can't be undone.
Your line: the greatest conquest. Today, when the small fight starts, take one breath before you act. Win it once. Day one hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often quote verse one hundred three to describe practice as an inner victory, and 'Jina,' the conqueror, is one of the traditional titles of the Buddha.

fork.setup: someone says something sharp to you in a meeting. the reply is already on your tongue. what would the greatest conqueror do?
options: pause for one breath before answering.
say nothing now and win it later by email.
fork.reveal: the conquest the verse praises is inner: the breath before the reply is the battle, and it's the one that can't be undone.

original.note: Pali: conqueror, a title of the Buddha, the one who conquered himself.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'conquer yourself' means harsh self-discipline.
what it means: winning the small inner fights, like anger and craving, a victory no one can take back.
what a scholar hears: verse 103's 'ekanca jeyyamattanam, sa ve sangamajuttamo': one who conquers the single self is the supreme victor in battle.

sources.quoted: If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.

notes: The commentary story for verses 102–103 (Kundalakesi) is not told.
Jina as a Buddhist title and its Jain use mentioned briefly as a neighbor, not a comparison.
The Buddha's upbringing as a prince trained in martial arts follows traditional biographies; kept as 'the stories say'.
